title: Spectral projections: selecting whole pieces of an operator
subtitle: G2 lecture 030000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Expanded companion deck developed from the spoken lecture and display-only mathematical appendix. Adds explicit mathematical formulas, worked examples, and topic-specific diagrams while remaining standalone.

slides.title: The central construction
slides.lead: Davis–Kahan asks about whole spectral subspaces, not one eigenvector at a time.
body: For a finite-dimensional self-adjoint matrix, the spectral theorem splits the space into orthogonal eigenspaces. A spectral projection is the operator that keeps the components whose eigenvalues lie in a chosen set and discards the rest.

This gives a coordinate-free way to say “keep the part of the vector belonging to this spectral cluster.” Later, perturbation theorems compare these selected subspaces before and after a perturbation.
slides.takeaway: A spectral projection is the canonical selector for a set of eigenvalues.

slides.title: Projecting onto one eigenspace
slides.lead: Start with a single eigenvalue λ and its eigenspace E_λ.
body: Because E_λ is a closed subspace in finite dimensions, there is an orthogonal projection P_λ onto it. Applying P_λ keeps the E_λ component of a vector and removes everything perpendicular to E_λ.
Idempotence says that projecting twice changes nothing after the first step. Self-adjointness records that this is an orthogonal, not oblique, projection.
slides.takeaway: Each eigenspace comes with its own orthogonal selector P_λ.

slides.title: Selecting a whole set S
slides.lead: Now choose any set S of real numbers and keep exactly the eigenspaces whose eigenvalues lie in S.
body: Numbers of S that are not eigenvalues do nothing. Only actual spectral components contribute. Because distinct eigenspaces of a self-adjoint operator are orthogonal, the sum is again an orthogonal projection.
Its range is the direct sum of the selected eigenspaces. That range is called the spectral subspace associated with S.
slides.takeaway: Spectral selection is determined by the operator and the set S, not by an arbitrary basis choice.

slides.title: A two-by-two calculation
slides.lead: Take A = [[2,1],[1,2]], whose eigenvalues are 3 and 1 with diagonal and antidiagonal eigendirections.
body: If S = (2,∞), only the eigenvalue 3 is selected, so we keep the diagonal direction. Applied to the vector (4,0), the projection returns (2,2).
If S = [0,2], only the eigenvalue 1 survives, and the output on (4,0) is (2,-2). Adding the two outputs recovers the original vector because the two selected pieces are orthogonal and complementary.
slides.takeaway: A spectral projection literally decomposes a vector into orthogonal spectral pieces.

slides.title: Endpoints can change the answer
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 030000 · Endpoints can change the answer
slides.lead: Open and closed intervals behave differently whenever an eigenvalue sits on the boundary.
body: For the same matrix, the rule “keep eigenvalues greater than or equal to 1” selects both eigenspaces and gives the identity. The rule “keep eigenvalues strictly greater than 1” excludes the eigenspace for 1 and keeps only the eigenspace for 3.

If we move a threshold through a region containing no eigenvalues, the projection stays constant. It changes only when the threshold crosses an eigenvalue, at which moment an entire eigenspace is gained or lost.
slides.takeaway: Boundary conventions matter exactly when the spectrum touches the boundary.

slides.title: Repeated eigenvalues are selected all at once
slides.lead: A set of eigenvalues cannot distinguish directions inside one repeated eigenspace.
body: If A = diag(4,4,1), then selecting the eigenvalue 4 keeps the entire two-dimensional eigenspace for 4. The associated spectral projection is diag(1,1,0).

You may project onto one line inside that plane, and such a line may even be invariant, but that line projection is not the spectral projection determined solely by the set {4}. Spectral selection includes or excludes a repeated eigenspace as a whole.
slides.takeaway: Spectral projections depend only on eigenvalues, so repeated eigenspaces are indivisible.

slides.title: Why P_S commutes with A
slides.lead: Applying A before or after the selector produces the same selected components.
body: Write a vector as the sum of its selected and unselected spectral components. If we project first and then apply A, every surviving component is multiplied by its eigenvalue. If we apply A first and then project, the same components survive with the same multipliers.
Therefore the range of P_S is invariant under A, and so is its orthogonal complement. A spectral subspace is therefore a reducing subspace.
slides.takeaway: Commutation is the operator-theoretic shadow of spectral selection.

slides.title: Selections obey set algebra
slides.lead: The projection identities mirror ordinary set operations.
slides.mathtex: P_S P_T = P_{S\cap T},\qquad P_{S\cup T}=P_S+P_T\ \text{if } S\cap T=\varnothing,\qquad P_{S^c}=I-P_S
body: A spectral component survives two consecutive selections exactly when its eigenvalue belongs to both sets, giving the intersection rule. Disjoint selections keep orthogonal families of eigenspaces, so the union projector is the sum.

Selecting the complement means keeping everything discarded by S, which gives I − P_S. These identities let us manipulate spectral regions at the operator level rather than restarting from coordinates each time.
slides.takeaway: Set operations on spectral regions become algebraic identities among projections.

slides.title: A first example of functional calculus
slides.lead: A spectral projection is what you get by applying an indicator function to the operator.
body: The indicator of S equals 1 on S and 0 outside. When applied through the spectral decomposition, it multiplies the λ-eigenspace by 1 if λ lies in S and by 0 otherwise.
That viewpoint places spectral projections inside the functional calculus. The next lecture makes this relation explicit for general functions f, not only indicators.
slides.takeaway: Spectral projections are the simplest nontrivial operator functions.

slides.title: What to remember
slides.lead: Reconstruct the operator from its spectral selectors before moving on.
body: For each eigenvalue, first understand the orthogonal projection onto its eigenspace. Then group those projections according to a chosen set S. The sum is an orthogonal projection whose range is the selected spectral subspace.
It commutes with A, respects set algebra, and changes only when the selection boundary crosses an eigenvalue. Those are precisely the facts later perturbation bounds will exploit.
slides.takeaway: A spectral projection keeps exactly the spectral pieces chosen by S and packages them as a reducing subspace.
